doc.title: Ted Piltzecker interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 10, 2019

title: Emotion in a jazz solo, impressionism and tuning in to the day
summary: Piltzecker says his daily state affects his playing, and talks about emotion, Schoenberg, impressionism and balancing intellect and feeling.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: What about the level of emotion in a jazz solo? I read over the years, I’ve read over the years jazz musicians play how they feel. Do you think the way you feel on any particular day affects significantly the way you improvise?

Yes. I do. And I have two responses to this. One about the idea of playing the emotions in general. I’m going to come back to that. But the idea of being tuned into your particular day and where you are. Every — we’re different this moment than you were ten minutes ago or at nine o’clock in the evening. If you’re tuned in you’re more responsive, you’re more alert, you might be — it’s time for dinner and I haven’t eaten, I’m hungry, I’m going to be a little bit less responsive, perhaps less articulate here. So you know where your limit is. Sometimes you can’t go as far as you did when you are at a peak moment. And you have to honor that and go with it. It’s a little frustrating sometimes. And then other times you tune in and you know you can push the envelope a little bit more you know. But if you’re on stage and you’re trying to do good you want to push the envelope a little bit beyond that envelope, fall down and recover quickly, just teetering on the edge. You don’t want to just stay back here in safe land. I’m hopeful — that line — what I’m getting at is that line changes.

So in terms of your emotion, your cognitive ability, your physical ability that day, that line is always moving around you know. You can’t run a marathon if you didn’t sleep or you have a bad knee or whatever. You have to be conscious of that situation and honor it. Sometimes it is frustrating and sometimes it’s exhilarating. In terms of playing emotion I don’t try to do things. I think I — there are certain composers and approaches to things where you try to extract emotion, where emotion is a detriment to the goal. We don’t even think like that in music, but Schoenberg might be — the idea of tension and release, it wasn’t something that he concerned himself with at all. I mean you know? You try to have this sameness or even if you look back in the music, although impressionistic music was emotional, there’s a kind of sameness about the amorphous nature of a whole tone scale. You don’t know where one is, and you don’t know where Do is, you know, where the tonality is. So in a certain sense it sort of messes with your definitive, “We are home now,” emotional resolution.

Right. And it makes it more murky which is the intention of impressionism, to suggest rather than describe. So, and then the other thing or emotions of course if you’re doing meditation or Buddhist people — you know I’m not a practicing Buddhist or anything,

but you know if you extract that from your — get rid of the longing you know, as they say, as it’s said, perhaps it can open up a little avenue to get to someplace else. You’re not distracted by the longings or emotions. But the first thing is, to answer your question more directly, I’m really taking this whole thing out, but yes, I think I am emotional when I play and it just sort of happens. I don’t try to do this or try to do that, but when a phrase gets to a certain place and there’s a dominant chord building up and you throw out some more plus nines and flat thirteens, and the drummer’s thrusting you know, if resolution happens of course it’s emotional. I mean I confess to being sort of old school in that way, and I guess I’m proud of that. You know that’s sort of who I am. Other people might be more wholly intellectual. But it’s a combination of things for me, to find that balance. I mean music is, jazz is a very intellectual endeavor you know.
It’s incredible. I’m obviously very emotional.
